column1: Practice origin story: why it was started and what need it hopes to address.
column2:
Ankahee did not begin as a business idea. It began with a question we kept coming back to: what might be different if people could access the right support at the right time?

Both of us have seen, personally and professionally, how much easier it can be to navigate difficult periods when you have the right people and the right kind of support around you. We have also seen how often people wait until things feel unbearable before reaching out. And often, it isn't because they don't know that help exists. There is something quieter underneath it, something we learn almost without noticing: Maybe I'm asking for too much. Maybe someone else needs it more. I should be able to handle this on my own.

We can become so used to carrying things quietly that we forget we are allowed to put some of them down.

We imagine a world where you do not have to wait until things feel unbearable to ask for support. A world where reaching out for help does not have to mean that something is wrong with you, that you are not capable of handling life, or that you are asking for too much. Sometimes life simply gets in the way. We all have moments when we need a little more support, and needing it does not make us any less capable of finding our way through.

This is part of what we wanted Ankahee to hold. A space where you don't have to justify your struggles before they are worthy of care. Where you can come in because something feels difficult, confusing, or simply worth understanding, without having to wait for it to become a crisis. Where counselling can be a part of your life without having to take over your life.

But our vision for Ankahee has always extended beyond the therapy room.

Life today can be strangely lonely. We can be surrounded by people and still feel disconnected, especially while navigating busy cities, changing relationships, work, family expectations, and distance from the communities we grew up in. We wanted to create something that recognises that our wellbeing does not exist in isolation. The people we love, the communities we belong to, our relationships with our roots, and the ways we understand ourselves all matter.

So we see Ankahee as one part of a wider support system. A place where you can pause, make sense of what you are carrying, understand the patterns you have developed, and reconnect with the people, values, places, and parts of yourself that matter to you. Sometimes that might mean therapy. Sometimes it might mean learning something new, finding language for an experience, sitting with other people who are going through something similar, or simply realising that you are not as alone in what you feel as you thought you were.

We want mental health support to feel more accessible, more human, and more woven into everyday life. To make room for prevention alongside intervention, and for care before things fall apart. To make asking for support feel less like an admission that you cannot cope and more like what it really is: **one of the ways we take care of ourselves.**

And ultimately, we don't want therapy to tell you that you cannot find your way through without it. Quite the opposite. We want the work to help you understand yourself well enough, and trust yourself enough, to feel capable of meeting life as it comes. To know what you need, recognise what helps, reach for support when you need it, and eventually feel that you can carry more of life on your own terms.

**Because needing a little support along the way does not mean you lack the capacity to find your way. Sometimes, we just need someone to walk beside us for a while, until we can feel our footing again.**
To make mental health understanding more accessible and meaningful, helping people move beyond labels and awareness towards self-understanding, intentional choices, and value-based action.

* A community where you don't have to wait until things feel unbearable to ask for support.
* A culture where seeking support is seen as a part of being human, not a reflection of weakness, incapability, or being a burden.
* A world where people feel supported in developing the understanding, agency, and confidence to navigate life's challenges in their own way.

column1: Three to six practice values with a short explanation of each:
column2:
Empowerment: We want therapy to leave you feeling more capable of being the person steering your own life. Life will inevitably throw some lemons our way, but we want you to feel that you have choices in how you respond to them, and that you are allowed to take up space in your own story.
Prevention: You do not have to wait until things become unbearable to deserve support. We believe mental health care can be something we turn to along the way, helping us understand ourselves, navigate challenges, and build support before we reach a crisis point.
Restoration: Sometimes things become overwhelming. You might reach a point where everything feels like too much, and knowing what to do next becomes difficult. We want therapy to be a space where you can come as you are, including when things already feel difficult to manage. Together, we can make sense of what is happening, find ways to get through the immediate challenges, and gradually help you feel more steady and capable again.
Alignment: We want therapy to help you understand what matters to you and make choices that feel more aligned with your values, needs, relationships, and the kind of person you want to be. There is not one right way to live a good life. The question is what feels right and meaningful for you.
Autonomy: We believe you are the person who knows your life from the inside. Therapy can offer another perspective, a place to pause, and someone to think things through with, but you remain the person steering the process. You get to decide what you need, what feels right for you, what you are ready for, and what you want your life to look like.
Acceptance: Some things in life are within our control, and some are not. We make space for both. Acceptance, for us, is not about giving up or settling. It's about understanding what we can change, making peace with what we cannot, and deciding where we want to put our energy.

Context & Intersectionality: People do not exist in isolation from their families, communities, cultures, identities, and systems. We consider how caste, class, gender, sexuality, family structures, social expectations, and other lived experiences can shape the ways we understand ourselves and move through the world. Your struggles don't exist outside of your context.

Humour: Therapy can hold difficult things without having to be serious all the time. We believe there should be room to laugh, be silly, find the absurdity in things, and bring your whole self into the room. Sometimes a little humour makes it easier to sit with something that otherwise feels very heavy.

column1: Therapeutic approach and modalities used. Explain these in client-friendly language.
column2:
Internal Family Systems (IFS): Think of your mind like a household where different "parts" of you show up in different situations: the part that people-pleases, the part that shuts down, the part that panics before a big decision. IFS helps you get to know these parts instead of fighting them, so they can work with you instead of running the show. Often used for anxiety, self-criticism, people-pleasing, and feeling pulled in different directions internally.

Cognitive Analytic Therapy (CAT)
CAT is like tracing the footpath you keep ending up on, even when you did not mean to walk it; the same argument, the same shutdown, the same choice in relationships. It helps you map where that pattern started and gives you room to choose a different path. Often used for repeating relationship patterns, low self-worth, and feeling stuck in cycles you can name but can't seem to break.

Trauma-Informed Counselling
This is not a specific technique so much as a way of working like adjusting the lighting and pace of a room so it actually feels safe to be in. Nothing is rushed, and you are never pushed to share more than you are ready to. Useful for traumatic experiences or overwhelming experiences, feeling on edge or shut down without knowing why, and difficulty trusting people or environments (especially common in experiences of abuse and neglect)

Dialectical Behaviour Therapy (DBT)
DBT is like a toolbox for the moments when emotions move faster than you can think (emotional dysregulation). It gives you concrete skills to ride out intensity without it taking over. Helpful for overwhelming emotions, impulsive reactions, self-harm urges, and relationships that swing between very close and very conflicted.

Cognitive Behaviour Therapy (CBT)
CBT works on the idea that thoughts, feelings, and actions are all connected like three gears turning each other. Shift one, and the others start to move too. Commonly used for anxiety, low mood, phobias, and unhelpful thought spirals ("everyone thinks I messed up," "I always do this").

Grief Therapy
Grief isn't a straight line you finishrather  it's more like weather, it comes in waves, changes shape, and doesn't disappear on a schedule. This work isn't about "getting over" a loss, but learning to carry it and live alongside it. Used for loss of a loved one, loss of a relationship, identity, or life as you knew it, and grief that doesn't look like what people expect it to.

column1: Inclusivity, accessibility, confidentiality, or cultural-sensitivity statement:
column2:
Inclusivity, Accessibility & Confidentiality

We want Ankahee to be a space where you can show up as you are, without having to leave parts of yourself at the door. We approach therapy with curiosity and respect for the different identities, cultures, families, relationships, and lived experiences that shape each person.

We offer therapy across English, Hindi, Marwari, and Nepali, and aim to make support as accessible and comfortable as possible. Our sessions are confidential, with the usual professional and ethical exceptions where safety may be at risk.

We also recognise that therapy should not be one-size-fits-all. We work collaboratively, taking your context, needs, preferences, and pace into account as we figure out what feels most helpful together.

column1: What makes the practice different from other therapy practices?
column2:
Thoughtful, Evidence-Based Therapy
Our work draws from approaches including Cognitive Analytic Therapy (CAT), Internal Family Systems (IFS), CBT, DBT, and trauma-informed practice. We shape therapy around you, your goals, and what feels most meaningful, rather than following a fixed method.
Understanding Beyond Symptoms
We believe our thoughts, emotions, and relationships don't exist in isolation. Together, we'll explore the experiences, relationships, and environments that have shaped your life, helping you understand recurring patterns and discover ways of responding that feel more supportive and intentional.
Grounded in the Realities of Everyday Life
Whether you're navigating family expectations, relationship dynamics, workplace stress, identity, or major life transitions, therapy makes space for the cultural, social, and personal contexts that shape your experiences.
Therapy in the Language You Think In
Sessions are available in English, Hindi, Marwari, and Nepali, making it easier to express yourself in the language that feels most natural.
Beyond the Therapy Room
Alongside therapy, we work with organisations, educational institutions, and mental health professionals through workshops, training programmes, and Employee Assistance Programmes (EAPs), making mental health conversations more accessible in the communities where people live, learn, and work.
